This raises a fundamental question: how can the quasiparticle picture be extended to open quantum systems to account for such phenomena and enable the experimental probing of quasiparticle spectra? Here we introduce coherent and incoherent Liouvillian quasiparticles, defined by responses to perturbations acting on one side and both sides of the density matrix, respectively. We propose spectroscopy protocols that couple the system to auxiliary levels, either coherently or via a dissipative pulse, to measure the corresponding complex quasiparticle energies. Numerical simulations of Liouvillians with skin effects validate these protocols, revealing nontrivial spectral winding associated with unidirectional transport in real space. Notably, coherent and incoherent quasiparticles can propagate in opposite directions within the same system. Furthermore, in models exhibiting weak and strong-to-weak $U(1)$ spontaneous symmetry breaking, our results unveil gapless Nambu-Goldstone modes in the coherent and incoherent quasiparticle spectra, respectively; the other quasiparticle spectrum remains gapped in each case. Our work provides a unified framework for theoretically describing and experimentally probing coherent and incoherent quasiparticles in open quantum many-body systems.

title: Compact and Long-Term Stable Polarization Entangled Photon-Pair Source
summary: We present a robust, compact polarization-entangled photon-pair source based on bulk optics that achieves long-term stability, a spectral pair generation rate of $4.24 \times 10^6$ pairs s$^{-1}$ mW$^{-1}$ nm$^{-1}$ constant for pump powers up to 700 mW, an intrinsic heralding efficiency of 59.8% , and a polarization contrast visibility of 99.6%. The source is mechanically designed for vibrational robustness, employing an engineered base plate and a reduced optical layout for less alignment sensitivity and complexity. It operates at telecom wavelengths in C-band with a typical type-0 SPDC spectral output of 70 nm width. We demonstrate its integration into a deployed entanglement-based QKD system that bridges the gap between laboratory prototypes and practical quantum communication hardware.

title: Self-consistent Floquet theory of steady-state ordering in driven open systems
summary: Periodically driven open systems have quasienergy bands whose steady-state occupations are set by the drive and reservoir. We formulate a self-consistent Floquet spectral theory of electronic ordering in the weak-reservoir-coupling limit, expressing the nonlinear mean-field equation and the particle-hole response in terms of quasienergies, steady-state occupations, and harmonic matrix elements that account for micromotion. We illustrate the theory in the square-lattice Hubbard model and show how the drive produces `dynamical nesting' conditions and how Floquet resonances produce \textit{hysteretic} responses due to multiple self-consistent solutions. Interestingly, we find that the hysteresis branches exhibit distinct Floquet topologies. Away from half-filling, we find that the combination of drive-induced detuning of the van Hove saddle points and the micromotion leads to the onset of switching between competing incommensurate orders.

title: Single-Phonon-Gated Pair Charging of Quantum Batteries
summary: Charging a quantum battery requires both an energy source and access to a channel through which that energy can be transferred. If that access depends on a quantum state, charging becomes conditional on the state while the external controls remain unchanged. We show that a single phonon in a common mechanical mode enables a second-order resonant pair transition in a two-cell battery formed by the electronic spins of two nitrogen-vacancy centers, whereas the mechanical vacuum supports no corresponding resonance. At fixed controls and mean phonon number, the final stored energy and ergotropy reached with a one-phonon Fock state are unattainable with any classical mixture of coherent states. An energy balance shows that the microwave drives supply nearly all of the stored energy, while the phonon contributes only a small fraction. Our results open a route to quantum-state-conditioned charging in quantum batteries under experimentally feasible parameters.

title: A Fractional Chern Semimetal: Exact Wavefunction and Conformal Criticality
summary: Unlike fractional quantum Hall states in uniform Landau levels, fractional Chern insulators can host dispersive anyon bands, raising the question of what happens when the anyon gap closes. We construct an exact finite-bond-dimension tensor-network state for a fractional Chern semimetal by Gutzwiller projecting a critical parton state. This state exhibits divergent correlation lengths in charged sectors but a fractionally quantized many-body Chern number of $1/3$. Although it has one electron per unit cell, its modular $S$ and $T$ matrices and entanglement spectrum match those of the $ν=1/3$ Laughlin state. We identify a $(1+1)$--dimensional $U(3)_1\times SU(3)_1$ conformal field theory (CFT) governing the wavefunction norm in the infrared, an unexpected result for a state with $U(1)_3$ topology. The $SU(3)_1$ sector is a nonlinear sigma model whose Wess--Zumino level and kinetic stiffness are determined by the parton Chern number and Fubini--Study metric, respectively. Under renormalization, it flows to the conformal fixed point, with an initial distance to this fixed point controlled by the idealness of parton quantum geometry. Favorable geometry enables precise agreement with CFT predictions even on narrow cylinders.

title: Undecidable quantum storage: no algorithm can tell from the noise rate whether a fixed circuit remembers
comment: 177 pages, 4 figures, 13 tables. Archive and Lean sources: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24254845
summary: Below a threshold noise rate, error correction lets larger quantum memories store a qubit for longer, without limit. Can the noise rate alone tell us whether a given noisy circuit does this? We construct fixed local circuits for which no algorithm can, already in one dimension under single-qubit noise. Each circuit is translation-invariant and time-periodic, with depolarizing noise on every wire after every layer, including all classical control. A computable list of disjoint rate intervals is indexed by the inputs $n$ of a universal Turing machine; local noise statistics select the input that the circuit simulates, and halting triggers erasure. If the machine runs forever on $n$, a qubit is stored throughout the $n$-th interval at entanglement fidelity at least $15/16$ for a time that grows without bound with size: linearly on rings, exponentially in six dimensions. The encoding and decoding maps are noiseless and global; they depend on $n$, the system size and, for decoding, the time, but not on the rate. If it halts, the fidelity of every encoding falls below $1/2+η$, for any fixed $η>0$, after a time independent of size and rate. The labels of the intervals with unbounded storage form a $Π^0_1$-complete set, and intervals of both kinds accumulate at zero, so these circuits have no noise threshold. Without rate selection, the ring construction is a translation-invariant, time-periodic memory: from an initialized classical hierarchy it stores a qubit for a time linear in the ring length at every sufficiently small rate, addressing the memory part of a one-dimensional question raised by Dünnweber, Styliaris and Trivedi. These are existence results: registers and interaction ranges are very large and the rates astronomically small.

title: Quantum-geometry-tuned Mott transition and emergent heavy fermions in a topological flat band
summary: A flat band with a nonzero Chern number has no localized Wannier orbitals, which raises the question of whether Mott physics is still possible. We place a Hubbard interaction $U$ on coherent orbitals, which are localized but overcomplete, and develop a single-site dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) for this model. Within the flat band alone, DMFT reproduces the experimentally observed cascade and inverse-compressibility sawtooth without invoking Dirac revival or remote-band electrons. At nonzero integer filling we find an insulator-to-metal transition tuned by $s^2$, the fraction of the Brillouin zone that carries the Berry curvature. For $N_f=8$ flavors the Mott transition at $ν=-2$ occurs at $s^2_c\approx0.025$, where the top of the lower Hubbard band reaches the Fermi level and the local moments are Kondo screened, forming a heavy Fermi liquid (HFL). The HFL extends to the hole-doped side, $ν=-2-x$, but above the small Kondo temperature $T_K$ the state is an incoherent bad metal without a Fermi surface. At low temperature, an anti-Hund's coupling $J_A\sim0.1U$ replaces the HFL with a pseudogap metal that has a small Fermi surface and is dominated by spin-polaron excitations at small $x$. We propose this pseudogap metal as the parent state of superconductivity in TBG. The framework may also be applied to other topological bands, such as those of twisted WSe$_2$.

title: Where to Hide the Traps: Robust Placement in Verifiable Blind Quantum Computation
summary: Trap-based verification of blind quantum computation hides test qubits among the positions of a measurement pattern, and existing protocols choose the trap configuration without regard to the delegated computation. We model trap placement as a zero-sum game between a client, who chooses a trap distribution, and a server, who chooses where to apply a Pauli deviation, with a damage profile $w$ and a per-trap detection constant $c$. Since the client cannot know how damage from several positions combines, we solve the game for all monotone subadditive damage functions consistent with $w$ at once. In a single round, placing traps in proportion to $w$ guarantees soundness error $1-c/\|w\|_1$ and is optimal up to a factor $1+\max_iw_i$, while the optimistic solution can fail completely. Over $T$ test rounds, the error decays exponentially against a server that repeats the same deviation, but a general server can keep it at $Θ(\|w\|_1/(cT))$, and against such servers the damage-weighted placement is exactly optimal. Damage profiles follow from the flow of the pattern: for brickwork patterns with $m=4h+1$ columns, only $(2h+1)^2$ positions can affect a decision qubit, whatever the width. With $k$ traps per round, placing them on this set reduces the number of test rounds by the same factor as for a single trap; with unrestricted trap sets and flat damage we recover the known optimality of fractional coloring. Finally, trap statistics certify the aggregate damage with a number of rounds independent of the number of positions $N$, whereas locating the damage requires $Ω(Nε^{-2}\logδ^{-1})$ rounds.

title: Quantum Geometric Tensor in Parameter-Dependent Quasi-Hermitian Systems
summary: A parameter-dependent physical inner product makes the comparison of quantum states at different parameter points non-unique. We formulate two geometric prescriptions for this comparison in quasi-Hermitian systems. The Type I QGT is defined by an inner-product-compatible covariant derivative and horizontal projection. It is a Hermitian, positive-semidefinite Gram tensor, and, for any normalized solution of the inner-product-preserving dynamics, its tangential component equals the physical energy variance. The Type II QGT is constructed from the endpoint overlap of physical dual states and is invariant under local $GL(1,\mathbb{C})$ rescalings. We show that, on a normalized section, it coincides with the established left--right (LR) QGT, while providing an endpoint-overlap interpretation of that tensor. Our central result is an exact relation between the two constructions: in the positive Dyson frame, the Type I QGT is the positive Gram block of the dressed-derivative sector, while the real symmetric part of the Type II QGT is this metric minus a positive-semidefinite contribution from the metric connection; the full complex tensor also contains cross terms. This relation clarifies the origin of the possible indefiniteness of the Type II metric and separates it from the positivity of the physical Hilbert-space metric. We further distinguish instantaneous Dyson mappings from the fixed inner-product-preserving dynamics and characterize the conditions under which the corresponding QGTs agree. Three two-level models illustrate these results. The physical content of the two tensors is then identified through the energy uncertainty and evolution speed for Type I, and the symmetrized endpoint overlap, complex holonomy, and signed dynamical response for Type II.

title: Approximation of Semigroups of Random Processes on a Hilbert Space
summary: This paper develops Chernoff-type approximation methods for strongly continuous and bi-continuous semigroups of operators arising in the stochastic dynamics of quantum systems. The main focus is on applying Chernoff iterations to Markov semigroups of multiplicative random processes on separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. The justification of the passage from discrete quantum measurements to continuous ones depends essentially on the choice of topology and function spaces. We propose conditions for convergence to bi-continuous semigroups on subspaces that weaken the classical requirements of the Chernoff theorem. The existence of the limiting bi-continuous semigroup is established in each of the three cases: commutation of the approximating operators, their asymptotic commutation, and uniform convergence of difference quotients over a family of approximating operators. For diffusive models with a generator having bounded coefficients, the derivative of the approximating function is computed explicitly on the subspace of test functions with rapidly decreasing second derivative; the limitations of applicability of this result are discussed. Applications to generalized models of continuous imprecise quantum measurement with unbounded observables, as well as to Poisson and diffusion processes, are outlined as directions for further research.

title: Optimizer or physics? Machine-learning surrogates for collision-based preparation of multipartite entangled quantum states
summary: Repeated partial-SWAP collisions can prepare symmetric Dicke states, including the $W$ state, without measurement or postselection. The collision sequence uses only two global collision angles, and its fidelity is evaluated after a final layer of local phase rotations is optimized numerically, so each candidate pair requires a many-qubit simulation and a phase fit. We study when learned surrogates reduce the number of such evaluations, and what limits the best-found fidelity, for 65 Dicke targets with 11--20 qubits in noiseless simulations. At 50 evaluations per target, Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization (GP-BO) exceeds fixed Sobol and grid designs by 0.088 and 0.063 in mean best-found fidelity. Bounded Nelder--Mead reaches 0.760 against 0.762 for GP-BO, and has the higher three-seed mean on 41 of the 61 targets with a reference value; in this two-parameter problem, adaptivity matters far more than the choice between the two methods. A neural-network ensemble pretrained on 750 observations from smaller systems needs 32\% fewer new evaluations per target than GP-BO at comparable fidelity, but the full neural search takes 1.6 times the wall time of GP-BO in our implementation. In a separate source-only test, the best of five neural proposals per target exceeds the best of five population-model proposals by 0.070 in mean fidelity. Exact symmetries and state diagnostics help explain why the leading adaptive methods reach similar family-mean fidelities. The collisions conserve the magnitude of the bare Dicke overlap and the total-spin weights, and for the best controls on a 12-target diagnostic panel, 79% of the infidelity is an amplitude deficit that a final phase layer cannot remove, which motivates interleaved phase control.

title: Bogoliubov-picture thermofield dynamics in anharmonic environments
summary: Thermofield dynamics (TFD) describes finite-temperature quantum relaxation through a purified wavefunction, without sampling thermally populated initial states. For harmonic environments, TFD is typically combined with a thermal Bogoliubov transformation to obtain a compact wavefunction representation. This transformation can also be useful for anharmonic baths, but preparing the corresponding thermal state in the transformed representation poses additional numerical challenges. Here, we explore TFD approaches tailored to anharmonic potentials and compatible with efficient tensor network methods for quantum propagation. We show that the conceptually appealing route of converting a harmonic-reference thermal state into the target anharmonic state by imaginary-time propagation can be numerically ill-conditioned. As a practical alternative, we formulate a multilayer multiconfiguration time-dependent Hartree (ML-MCTDH) protocol that separates thermal-state preparation from the harmonic-reference Bogoliubov transformation. We prepare the thermal purification in the bare representation and then apply finite-basis Bogoliubov unitaries to the physical--auxiliary mode pairs. For independent bath modes, direct construction of the thermal amplitude provides a complementary initialization procedure. We illustrate this protocol through vibrational relaxation and spatial-superposition decoherence of a harmonic subsystem coupled to a Morse-oscillator bath. We find non-monotonic energy relaxation, shifts in the dominant resonant response, and oscillatory energy exchange at zero and finite temperature. For decoherence, we recover the expected harmonic-bath scaling and find a pronounced non-monotonic dependence of the decay rate on anharmonicity at finite temperature in a low-frequency model, with a weaker dependence in a high-frequency model.

title: No-Go Theorems for Transversal and Automorphism Clifford Gates on Prime-Dimensional Qudit Stabilizer Codes
summary: Logical Clifford gates are a basic primitive of fault-tolerant quantum computation. For stabilizer codes on qudits of prime dimension $p$ that encode $k\geq 2$ logical qudits, we prove that Clifford gadgets that are transversal with respect to a fixed partition of the physical qudits into blocks of fewer than $k$ qudits cannot realize the full logical Clifford group, and that this block size is tight. Code automorphisms, which combine single-qudit Clifford gates with qudit permutations, also fail for every $p$. Both obstructions come from prime-order logical Clifford elements that these gadgets cannot reach.

title: Multi-port few-photon diodes
summary: We investigate single- and two-photon scattering dynamics in a system comprising two one dimensional chiral waveguides coupled to a dissipative Rydberg atom pair. By employing the Laplace transform method, we analytically solve the scattering problem and characterize the transport properties. Our results demonstrate robust perfect single-photon diode effects in this system with or without dissipation, exhibiting unity transmittance in the forward direction and zero transmittance in the backward direction. Unlike previous studies where perfect nonreciprocity requires a specific dissipation rate, our scheme achieves this effect without fine-tuning such parameters. Furthermore, we extend the nonreciprocal transport to multi-port configurations at the one and two-photon levels. The system exhibits pronounced photon nonreciprocal behavior in lossy and lossless scenarios, without the need for precise parameter matching. This work provides a robust platform for on-chip nonreciprocal photonic devices.

title: Scaling of phase rigidity without eigenstate coalescence
summary: Phase rigidity vanishes as a power law near exceptional points, reflecting the coalescence of eigenstates at these points. In this Letter, we show that non-Hermitian skin effects induce distinct asymptotic behaviors of phase rigidity without eigenstate coalescence. To demonstrate this, we derive exact analytical results for three non-Hermitian chain models and verify them numerically. For the ordinary skin effect, phase rigidity decays exponentially with increasing system size $N$, as the right and left eigenstates are exponentially localized at opposite boundaries. For the scale-free skin effect, phase rigidity exhibits an $N^{-2}$ power-law approach to a nonzero constant as the right and left eigenstates have decay lengths proportional to $N$. For the algebraic skin effect studied here, phase rigidity can exhibit an $N^{-1/2}$ power-law decay to zero, with the right eigenstate algebraically localized near a boundary and the left eigenstate spread across the chain. These findings show that non-Hermitian skin effects govern phase-rigidity scaling by shaping the spatial profiles of the right and left eigenstates, enabling control of eigenstate nonorthogonality without exceptional points.

title: A single-photon quantum sensor via single-atom cavity-QED
summary: We describe a cavity-QED sensor using an optical probe with exactly one photon per pulse. This has a better sensitivity than a coherent pulse with the same average power when no global coherent phase reference is available. The sensor measurement is based on the estimation of the Raman-controlled absorption probability of a single-photon pulse. We use the Fock state master equation to determine the dynamics and performance of the Raman-controlled absorption of a single photon pulse and optimise the sensitivity using machine learning. Two examples are presented; (1) the target parameter is the detuning of the two-level system itself, and (2) the target parameters describe a remote reflecting cavity. In the second case, the scheme does not require a shared coherent phase reference.

title: Unveiling the Action of Randomized Compiling on Quantum States: A Geometric Perspective
summary: Randomized compiling (RC) converts coherent errors into stochastic Pauli noise, but this conversion alone does not imply isotropic contraction of the output state. Here we use the generalized Bloch vector (GBV) representation to examine the cumulative effect of RC on state purity and orientation in multi-layer circuits. For the independent, isotropically distributed weak coherent errors considered here, the accumulated ensemble-averaged RC channel lies close to the depolarizing direction, producing a state-level near-isotropic contraction that sacrifices a small amount of purity to achieve a substantial suppression of orientational deviation. When dephasing coexists, RC suppresses the coherent-error contribution but leaves a residual deviation dominated by dephasing, setting a limit that we term the "dephasing wall". We experimentally validate these findings on a superconducting quantum processor through GHZ state preparation and phase estimation in a simulation of topological braiding. The results confirm that RC's effectiveness stems from its ability to suppress the orientational bias of coherent errors---a structural transformation not resolved by fidelity alone but directly visible through GBV diagnostics.

title: Interaction-Driven Photocurrent Enhancement in a Quantum Photocell with Opposite Transient and Steady-State Responses
summary: We study photocurrent control in a quantum photocell with interacting qubit-qutrit donors coupled to an acceptor. We show that stronger Heisenberg exchange coupling and anisotropy increase the transient photocurrent but reduce its steady-state value, whereas the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction favors steady-state output at the expense of transient enhancement. This reversal highlights the need to distinguish rapid current generation from sustained operation when tuning quantum photovoltaic devices. Analysis of donor purity further reveals that the qutrit's local purity tracks the photocurrent trends in both regimes. These results demonstrate that the effects of donor interactions depend crucially on the timescale of operation, suggesting a strategy for tailoring the response of hybrid quantum photocells to different operating regimes.

title: On-demand frequency-entangled microwave biphotons from a transmon-resonator dimer
summary: We propose a superconducting circuit QED source of on-demand frequency-entangled microwave photon pairs, with one photon emitted into each of two separate waveguides, enabling individual manipulation. The design is based on a transmon-resonator dimer, which consists of two transmon-resonator subsystems coupled through a cross-Kerr interaction. We outline a viable circuit-QED realization in which the required cross-Kerr interaction is implemented using Josephson-junction couplers. To analyze the emission dynamics, we derive and numerically solve the set of evolution equations that enable tracking the evolution of the joint spectral intensity of photons. We characterize the resulting photon-number correlations, frequency anticorrelation, and spectral entanglement. By varying the coupling strengths, we obtain biphotons with distinct joint spectral intensities and Schmidt spectra, ranging from broadly distributed multimode entanglement to states dominated by two nearly equally weighted Schmidt contributions. In the latter regime, optimizing the transmon-resonator coupling and detuning yields an output biphoton state that has fidelity $F \approx 0.956$ with a two-dimensional maximally entangled state. Restricting the local target modes to separated frequency bins yields a fidelity $F_\mathrm{bin} \approx 0.949$, indicating that the output state closely approximates a frequency-bin Bell pair. Thus, the proposed microwave biphoton source provides a route toward distributing frequency-encoded quantum resources between remote superconducting nodes.

title: Differentiable collision-model control for multipartite state engineering: reachability, geometry, and preparation cost
summary: We study a differentiable control architecture for multipartite state engineering in which partial-SWAP collisions, a Heisenberg exchange, are interleaved with layers of local phase rotations. Singular collision angles confine the evolution to invariant supports, impose exact fidelity ceilings, and generate an inverse-distance lower bound on the preparation time nearby. Away from them, numerical certificates show that the sampled couplings reach the whole fixed-excitation sector for sector dimensions up to 21, and optimizations reach fidelities above 0.999 for dimensions up to 1716. At generic couplings the number of rounds needed for a given Dicke fidelity, measured by the ratio of independent phase controls to the projective dimension, is nearly independent of the system size, and the quantum Fisher information spectrum is close to that of a random Gaussian Jacobian. Near full SWAP, a slow-time theory, the sharp form of the inverse-distance bound there, predicts microscopic hitting times without fitted parameters: the distance from the singular point sets the clock and its direction selects the effective control geometry. A detuning sweep along two rays shows that the Dicke horizon follows this law up to a detuning of 0.1, where it is two to five times shorter than at a generic coupling in sectors of dimension 70 to 252, while phase-uniform, random-sign, and Haar-random targets are delayed; beyond a detuning of about 0.3 all targets return to the generic cost. The slow-time value for the Dicke target is nearly the same for sector dimensions from 35 to 252. The exchange graph of the effective theory offers an interpretation of this ordering. Counted in two-qubit gates, generic-coupling preparation is costlier than known Dicke circuits; the architecture offers fixed global couplings, local phase rotations as the only control, and no measurement.

title: Non unitary and nonlinear quantum generative large model design and fast large-scale training without back propagation
summary: Transformer-based large models require huge computational and storage costs. Quantum computation is expected to address that due to its potential to speed up classical algorithms exponentially. Key challenges of implementing quantum large models include the linear, unitary nature of qubit evolutions contrast with the non-unitary matrices and nonlinear functions in classical Transformers, as well as the difficulty of implementing gradient back-propagation on quantum hardware. Here we propose a fully quantum large model containing all the Transformer layers, implementing the non-unitary transformations through SVD-decomposition-based quantum circuits, and approximated nonlinear activation functions through pre-trained parameterized quantum circuits. We also propose a quantum circuit training algorithm based on multi-agent Reinforcement Learning, which can train large-scale parameterized quantum circuits without back-propagation. The dependency between the inference time complexity and the model's hidden dimension has been reduced from polynomial to logarithmic, showing an exponential advantage. The inference executions on the quantum hardware verify our model's 300-1000 times speed-up, and the measurements on the sequence-to-sequence tasks shows its learning ability. The training algorithm achieves only 25% complexity of the best SOTA quantum circuit training algorithms, especially this ratio decreases fast as the parameter scale increases. Our work not only proposes a quantum large model that can significantly reduce the computational cost, but also promotes the quantum computation towards general computing.

title: Feed-Forward Dimension Control for High-Dimensional Quantum Key Distribution over Time-Varying Airborne Free-Space Links
summary: High-dimensional quantum key distribution tolerates more noise than qubit-based protocols, but the dimension that maximizes the secret key depends on turbulence, background light, device imperfections, and block size, all of which change during an airborne or satellite pass. Finite-size security analyses of high-dimensional protocols fix the dimension in advance, and the dimension-adaptive schemes reported so far have been analyzed only asymptotically. Here, a controller sets the dimension, acceptance thresholds, and key length of each block using only public data from earlier blocks. Each block is therefore a standard fixed-length protocol, and composable finite-key security against coherent attacks follows from sequential composition; an inaccurate channel model reduces the key rate but does not weaken security. The controller estimates turbulence from observed error rates, maximizes the expected key under forecast uncertainty, and recalibrates its model online. We evaluate it on a simulated entanglement-based orbital-angular-momentum link between an aircraft and a ground station, using Kolmogorov phase screens and the Hufnagel--Valley turbulence profile. Accounting for forecast uncertainty increases the key by 31\%--47\% relative to a naive planner. Over night, dawn, daytime, and model-mismatch scenarios, the recalibrated controller retains at least 98.8\% of the key obtained with the best fixed dimension for each scenario, while every fixed dimension drops to 73.5\% or less in at least one scenario. Running the link's measurement statistics on a superconducting quantum processor shows device errors close to a constant offset; with these errors included, the best daytime dimension changes from eight to four, and the controller adjusts accordingly.

title: Just another Markovian embedding for open quantum systems
summary: In this work, I present one more method for analysis of non-Markovian open quantum systems by embedding them into larger Markovian systems. As many other approaches, this method starts from finding a rational approximation for the bath correlation function in the frequency domain, the difference is that I retain $ω\to -\overline ω$ symmetry for the poles of the approximation. This allows to reduce the dimension of embedding from one- to half-degree-of-freedom per pole. In case of odd number of poles, the resulting equation describing dynamics of the system turns out to be not a Lindblad, but a hybrid quantum-classical master equation.

title: Network contextuality beyond binary outcomes
summary: Can a joint measurement reveal nonclassical behaviour in independently prepared systems that share no entanglement? We study network contextuality by extending the two-qubit test of bi-contextuality [G. Ruffolo et al., arXiv:2507.08461 (2025)] to projective measurements with more than two outcomes. In one laboratory, an observer measures the systems individually or jointly performs two compatible global measurements constructed from them. The individual probabilities constrain the possible classical correlations at each source. For our preparations, every noncontextual model with outcome-deterministic and source-independent assignments predicts a nonzero average product of the two global outcomes. The joint quantum measurement gives zero. We construct explicit product states realizing this contradiction for $N=d$ independent sources, each preparing one $d$-dimensional system, with $2\leq d\leq9$. We derive an inequality in observed probabilities, prove its single-source bounds are exact for these preparations, and give sufficient thresholds for violations under independent depolarizing noise. For this family of preparations the dimension range is sharp: for every $d\geq10$ the individual probabilities admit a zero assigned average, so the certificate fails. The same data admit a noncontextual explanation when source independence is relaxed.

title: Direct quantum simulation of compressible Navier-Stokes flow via finite homotopy linearisation
summary: We develop a direct quantum simulation algorithm for finite homotopy approximations to the non-isothermal compressible Navier-Stokes equations. A primitive-variable formulation gives polynomial residuals in the fields and their spatial and time derivatives, including density-weighted time derivatives. On a periodic grid, applying each spatial stencil uniformly to every factor in a shifted product preserves the dynamics of the finite homotopy hierarchy in an affine linearisation. Because each deformation equation depends only on lower homotopy orders, the lifted generator matrix is strictly block lower-triangular and hence nilpotent. The resulting finite-polynomial solution evaluates the final state directly without time-stepping error, while explicit short-time convergence conditions bound the homotopy truncation error on a fixed grid. In two-dimensional Taylor-Green flow, initial pressure balance removes the leading longitudinal acceleration and delays the onset of dilatational kinetic energy from quadratic to quartic in time. At Mach numbers 0.2 and 0.4, the fifth-order hierarchy reproduces viscous dissipation over a longer interval than pressure-dilatation at the same relative tolerance. We identify auxiliary variables representing the same evolving product, compile the finite-polynomial evolution into logical quantum circuits, and recover a signed velocity Fourier mode via Hadamard interference. Together, the Taylor-Green energy budgets quantify the accuracy windows of each homotopy order, while coarse-grid circuits verify the signed readout and measure gate counts. For higher-order evolution on finer grids, merging coincident stencil terms and combining block-encoded products along strictly increasing homotopy-order paths substantially reduce the predicted normalisation cost.

title: Quantum tomography of ququart states of optical vector vortices based on measurements in mutually unbiased bases
summary: In this paper we present an original method for quantum state tomography of vector optical vortices with an axially symmetric transverse polarization profile. We present an interference technique which allows one to distinguish states of vector vortices with a fixed topological charge with high accuracy. We also demonstrate the feasibility of experimental quantum tomography of the density matrix in the logical ququart space built on vector vortices, with high fidelity for all 20 basis states. It is shown that the proposed tomography scheme provides a uniform characterization of states in all mutually unbiased bases of the ququart space.

title: Extraction erases the gain: cavity loss bounds dynamical-Casimir metrology at ultrastrong coupling
comment: 26 pages, 10 figures, 9 tables; Supplemental Material included (25 pages)
summary: Ultrastrong light--matter coupling dresses the vacuum with virtual photons whose response to the coupling strength exceeds that of any coherent probe, yet these photons never leave the cavity and cannot be detected. A parametric drive at the dynamical-Casimir resonance converts them into real photons that a detector can collect. We show that this conversion is self-limiting: converting the virtual photons of an ultrastrongly coupled probe into real, extractable photons opens the cavity port that removes them, so the retained metrological gain is set by the accumulated cavity loss rather than by the pure-state ceiling. In the driven quantum Rabi model the pure-state quantum Fisher information on the coupling reaches $1.7\times10^{5}$ times the coherent baseline; at a cavity linewidth of $246$~MHz, typical of coplanar-waveguide flux-qubit circuits, master-equation dynamics retain $0.96\%$ of it. In a 32-qubit Dicke model the retained fraction is $2.6\%$ at the largest photon basis computed. Eighteen lossy configurations from both models fall on one curve of the accumulated loss, the product of linewidth and interrogation time, which halves the retained information at $0.13$. The extraction cost, not the lossless ceiling, is the figure of merit for any protocol that reads bound vacuum correlations through a lossy port.

title: Controlled Continuous-Time Quantum Walks for Power Grid Analysis under N-x Contingencies
summary: The combinatorial growth of network configurations under N-x contingencies presents significant computational challenges for power system analysis. In this work, we introduce a quantum algorithm based on Controlled Continuous-Time Quantum Walks (CCTQWs) that evolves a quantum walker conditioned on a contingency register held in a uniform superposition of all x-line outage configurations representing the contingency scenarios. The proposed framework encodes transmission line availability in a quantum register and employs controlled Hamiltonian evolution to account for topology changes induced by contingencies. We develop a gate-based implementation using Trotter-Suzuki product formulas and investigate the associated approximation errors and computational requirements. As a demonstration of the proposed methodology, we introduce a contingency-averaged occupation centrality measure derived from quantum-walk measurement statistics. Numerical experiments on an 8-bus power network under N-2 contingencies demonstrate the implementation of the algorithm and characterize the convergence of the resulting centrality estimates with respect to the observation window, sampling and Trotter steps. Comparison with established classical centrality measures shows a qualitatively consistent characterization of network structure, particularly in identifying the most central nodes. The proposed framework establishes a methodological foundation for quantum-walk-based analysis of power networks under contingencies, providing a starting point for future investigations of quantum algorithms for power system security assessment.

title: Improved two-way capacity upper bounds for amplitude-damping channels
summary: We derive an improved upper bound on the two-way-assisted capacities of the qubit amplitude-damping channel with decay probability $γ$, given by $\log_2[1+(1-γ)γ^{γ/(1-γ)}]$. It applies to quantum communication, entanglement distribution, private communication, and secret-key agreement, and, for every $0<γ<1$, strictly improves the PLOB relative-entropy bound, the analytic max-relative-entropy bound, and the optimized balanced squashed-entanglement bound. At high damping, a known triple-rail protocol attains more than $99.54\%$ of its leading coefficient. Our method extends sector teleportation simulation to qubits: phase rotations and permutations give exact simulations within fixed-excitation subspaces while preserving the two-level input structure. We determine the exact, additive relative entropy of entanglement of the amplitude-damping resources and the exact regularized entanglement gain at fixed input population. We then derive explicit bounds for generalized amplitude damping, which includes thermal excitation. Combining the amplitude-damping gain with unital and entanglement-breaking channels gives a closed expression that recovers the zero-temperature result and vanishes throughout the entanglement-breaking region. It improves established benchmarks over broad parameter ranges, while the exact entanglement of the generalized resources remains open. Both results admit refinements under an average-excitation constraint. The bounds provide quantitative limits for adaptive communication through relaxing qubits and show how a sector simulation can remain useful beyond channels whose resource entanglement is known exactly.

title: Local redundancies are necessary for long-lived memories in finite spatial dimensions
summary: We prove a no-go theorem for exponentially long-lived thermal memories, based on the structure of redundancies among Hamiltonian terms. For local stabilizer Hamiltonians in finite spatial dimensions, the absence of local redundancies---relations in which the product of a small number of Hamiltonian terms equals the identity---is known to preclude bulk thermodynamic phase transitions. Yet glassy dynamics can still sustain long-lived memories even without a thermodynamic transition, as demonstrated by LDPC codes on non-Euclidean graphs. A longstanding question, exemplified by Haah's cubic code, is whether such a mechanism can also support passive (quantum) memory in finite-dimensional Euclidean systems. We show that this route fails for local stabilizer Hamiltonians without local redundancies: at any constant nonzero temperature, local heat-bath dynamics is fast mixing, with $O(N)$ mixing time, where $N$ is the number of qubits. We establish this by proving a strong decay of correlations property of the thermal Gibbs state. We further prove rapid mixing with $O(\log N)$ mixing time under a stronger condition on induced redundancies in suitably chosen regions. This stronger result applies to several well-studied examples, including Haah's cubic code and its generalizations, as well as three-dimensional layer codes. Our work identifies redundancy structure as a key property for understanding thermal memories.

title: What can a quantum network promise about the entangled pairs it delivers?
comment: 47 pages, 9 figures, 12 tables. Code, pre-registrations and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24447997
summary: Quantum networks will give users entangled pairs of qubits, the resource behind teleportation and quantum-secure keys. But a user cannot check a pair without destroying it, so networks promise the quality of each pair, its fidelity, from a physical model rather than from a measurement. If the model is too optimistic, the delivery rule alone may miss the error. We ask: what can a network actually guarantee? Our main result has two sides. By testing some pairs at random, in secret, users can put a lower bound on the average fidelity of the pairs they keep, without any model and at every moment. But when they test only a small fraction and keep most pairs, the tests cannot reliably show that every kept pair meets a fidelity threshold: a rare bad pair can still slip through. A promise about every single pair therefore rests on a model, and we give a rule that bounds each user's risk of ever receiving a bad pair under any data-driven routing, as long as the model is not optimistic or a large enough margin is declared in advance. Real data show calibration noise beyond chance, and in simulated networks a model error of the size seen in one experiment breaks the per-pair promise unless the margin was declared. On real data from trapped-ion and diamond links, the number of pairs decided how strong the certificate was: with about 3,000 pairs of a kilohertz link and 20% tested, the median certificate was 0.818, against the 0.817 we predicted in advance. We then ran the protocol ourselves on a 36-qubit trapped-ion processor in 50 pre-registered jobs. The certificate came within 0.003 of the measured fidelity, dropped by the predicted amount when we secretly damaged a third of the pairs, and, without changes, certified three- and four-qubit entangled states. The same tests also catch an optimistic model, but slowly. We pre-registered every confirmatory analysis and report the failures too.

title: Stopping-Time Leakage in Blind Quantum Delegation
summary: Blind quantum computation lets a client delegate a computation while hiding it from the server, up to a declared leakage. Its security definitions cover a single round. A variational quantum algorithm, however, delegates many rounds, and its classical optimizer decides from private data when to stop. We study what the resulting round count tells an honest-but-curious server. For protocols with one-time-padded transcripts and fresh randomness in every round, we prove that the server's best distinguishing advantage over the whole sequence equals the total-variation distance between the stopping-time distributions, so the round count is the only residual channel in this model. We also show that soundness composes as $δ\,\mathbb{E}[T]$ under adaptive stopping, given a conditional per-round soundness property that composably secure verifiable protocols provide. In simulated delegated eigensolvers for the transverse-field Ising chain, the local Polyak-Lojasiewicz ratio measured in iterations 5 to 15 predicts the noiseless stopping round with a leave-one-out error of 1.7 iterations, compared with 10.3 for a constant predictor. Across 14 configurations that differ in optimizer, stopping rule, initialization, system size, shot budget and problem family, the leakage is significant in 12 and ranges from 0.14 to 1.68 bits, and a maximum-entropy bound estimated on held-out sessions lies above it in all of them. For defense, we show that any mechanism acting after the stopping decision can only add rounds, and that differentially private padding costs the full adjacency radius. A fixed public iteration budget removes the channel completely; set at the median run length, it costs 10% of the remaining energy gap. A differentially private stopping rule based on AboveThreshold protects every pair of instances, but it must often stop too early, which makes it costly.

title: Estimating a Transition Point from Gibbs and Ground States
summary:
We study how observed many-body system size affects the number of state copies needed to estimate a zero-temperature first-order transition point. The unknown Hamiltonian has bounded, translation-invariant on-site and nearest-neighbour interactions on a 3D cubic lattice with local dimension three. The field coupling is known, and all models share a known boundary field penalizing one local level. The limiting order parameter is uniformly separated across the transition. Each query returns an independently prepared Gibbs or ground state at an adaptive field and system size.
  For error $ε$ and fixed confidence, we prove an exponential separation between two size caps at the same temperature. There are absolute constants $0<c_0<C$ and $c_1>0$ such that, at inverse temperature $β=c_1/ε$, restricting side lengths to $L\le c_0/ε$ requires $\exp(Ω(1/ε))$ copies in worst-case expectation, even with collective measurements. Allowing $L\le C/ε$ permits $O(\log^2(1/ε))$ copies and $O(ε^{-3})$ total spins, using local measurements and polynomial classical postprocessing. The minimax expected total spin count is $Θ(ε^{-3})$ uniformly for $β\ge c_1/ε$. At fixed positive temperature it is $Θ_β(ε^{-2})$, attained from one- and eight-site Gibbs states followed by exponential classical computation. For ground-state copies it is $Θ(ε^{-3})$.
  The lower bound uses a three-state ferromagnet whose boundary suppresses the sector carrying transition information. A spanning-forest argument and edge-boundary counting control its Gibbs weight uniformly over fields and allowed sizes, and a trace-distance hybrid argument handles adaptive learners with quantum memory. The upper bound combines finite-volume free-energy estimates, concavity and local order-parameter measurements.

title: Joint Dynamics of Spins and Frequency-Resolved Bosonic Occupations: A Projection-Operator Approach
summary: We derive weak-coupling kinetic equations for frequency-resolved bosonic mode occupations in the spin--boson model. Rather than integrating out the bath completely, we retain these mode occupations as independent dynamical variables whose equations are coupled to those for the spin observables. A projection-operator construction closes the dynamics on a product-spin ansatz and an undisplaced Gaussian environment with a diagonal covariance matrix. The equations are obtained to second order in the interaction parameter $λ$ for an arbitrary number of spins within this factorized closure, and are solved numerically for a single spin. A fixed-truncation calculation using the hierarchical equations of motion provides a benchmark for the spin dynamics with the Drude--Lorentz spectral density. The numerical results reveal a redistribution of bosonic mode occupations concentrated near the spin transition frequency $Ω=\sqrt{Δ^2+h^2}$. We also examine the response of the coupled spin--boson system to structured spectra, nonthermal initial occupations, and slow modulation of the coupling. The calculated mode occupations also allow changes in the bath-side occupation and energy densities $p(ω)δ\langle N_ω\rangle(t)$ and $ωp(ω)δ\langle N_ω\rangle(t)$ to be obtained without requiring an exponential decomposition of the bath correlation function. Its scope is restricted to weak coupling, diagonal Gaussian bath states, and, for time-dependent couplings, the adiabatic regime.

title: When Does Fine-Tuning Beat Prompting for Qiskit-to-CUDA-Q Translation? An Execution-Verified Study
comment: 18 pages, 1 figure, 11 tables. Code, data and results: https://github.com/anapaulaappel/qiskit-to-cudaq
summary: Moving quantum code from Qiskit to NVIDIA CUDA-Q is a practical adoption cost that language models are starting to automate. We ask whether a small open model can learn this translation, and how to measure it so that the result can be trusted. Both programs can be executed and their state vectors compared, so a kernel counts as correct only if it prepares the same state as the Qiskit reference (fidelity >= 0.999), with no text matching and no LLM judge. We build a 640-task benchmark with three test sets (larger circuits, an unseen circuit family, an unseen Qiskit coding style) and a QuantumKatas regression probe, and we test the evaluator before training. Measurement counts miss every phase-only error; a surface rule-based translator solves two of three original splits (text substitution); a converter that executes the Qiskit input and maps the circuit solves all 640 tasks -- so the benchmark measures source-level translation, not whether a circuit can be ported after running it. No base model emits a valid CUDA-Q kernel zero-shot. On Nemotron 3 Nano 4B, LoRA reaches 83.9%, tying a 4-shot prompt (83.1%), but generalizes worse to unseen style (48.5% vs. 65.5%) and cuts QuantumKatas from 23.8% to 8.9%; on Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, LoRA beats the prompt overall (92.0% vs. 82.8%) and on unseen style (78.5% vs. 65.0%), and on the 1.5B model as well, so whether fine-tuning pays off depends on the base model, while the Qiskit regression appears in all three. Mixing two replay formats is the best mitigation trade-off (84.4% translation, Katas 21.5%). On 48 parametric functions that must become kernels with arguments -- where executing the input cannot yield a parametric kernel -- models reach up to 83%; on 27 real QED-C kernels, every model scores 0%. Language models can do source-level translation of simple parametric code, but not yet of real programs.

title: Quantum-Memory Forensics for Tampered Quantum Seals: Resource-Dependent Sample Gains
comment: 34 pages (24 pages main text + 10 pages supplementary information), 11 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Quantum Engineering
summary: Quantum seals reveal that an object was disturbed, but not where, with which tool, or when the tool changed. We study quantum-memory forensics for sealed items returning through an untrusted network where one tool opens many. Each seal cell is half of a Bell pair whose partner the verifier keeps in a protected quantum memory, a secret Pauli frame turns any attack into a Pauli channel, and a three-tier report localizes the tampering, learns a hidden-parity fingerprint of the tool and detects a tool switch in arrival order, not necessarily in attack order. Attribution concerns attackers who do not erase that fingerprint, which a random Pauli layer would do cheaply. Each result is stated within one of four verifier classes. For per-unit verifiers, which never couple two seal units and hold no untouched reference, the sample separation is asymptotically exponential, by reduction from a known lower bound for one parity of strength up to 1/3. On ten tampered cells it is proved to be at least \qnProvedUniformMin-fold against non-adaptive stabilizer probes and observed in simulation at \qnEoneRatioFine-fold. Against an implemented self-referencing strategy the simulated gain is about twice the inverse squared strength. The value also depends on the attack: destroying the untouched cells makes the reference necessary, whereas copying errors exposes the fingerprint to reference-free probes. We derive the vault's qubit inventory and simulate a seal requirement curve: ten times more seal noise lengthens the seal's lifetime \qnSealLifeGainFive-fold at \qnSealRhoFive{} times the attribution cost at $r=10$.

title: Generalized Bloch Oscillations of Doublon Defect in One-dimensional Antiferromagnetic Atomic Spin Chain under Linear and Quadratic Magnetic Gradients
summary: We investigate generalized Bloch oscillations of a single doublon defect in a one-dimensional antiferromagnetic $t$-$J_{\rm{z}}$ chain subjected to linear and quadratic magnetic field gradients. By mapping the spin-charge coupled many-body dynamics onto an effective single-particle model, we reveal how the Néel background mediates parity-dependent coupling between the defect and the external fields. The linear gradient induces a staggered potential that splits the Wannier-Stark ladder into two intertwined subladders, producing a characteristic beating pattern in the center-of-mass motion with a subband offset accurately captured by third-order perturbation theory. The quadratic gradient generates sublattice-dependent tilts that shear the ladder into a scissor-like profile, yielding site-dependent beating periods that encode the nonlocal spatial averaging of the defect wave function. When both gradients coexist, their interplay is fundamentally nonadditive: the quadratic gradient breaks the two-site periodicity that forbids second-order linear responses, unlocking a dominant cross-coupling proportional to $B_{\rm{z,1}}B_{\rm{z,2}}$. This leaves distinct fingerprints on the Bloch-oscillation spectrum---a rigid baseline hift of the fundamental doublet and asymmetric broadening of the first harmonic. These predictions are quantitatively corroborated by exact many-body simulations of the real-time density evolution and center-of-mass dynamics. Our work establishes a gradient-induced unlocking mechanism for multi-gradient defect spectroscopy in quantum magnets, offering a framework for probing parity-protected selection rules and their controlled breaking via generalized Bloch oscillations in tunable quantum simulators.

title: Proposal for a cat-cluster-state machine gun
summary: Non-Gaussian bosonic states such as the Schrödinger cat states are essential for continuous-variable quantum-information processing. A convenient and deterministic process for generating cat states is through the use of a Rabi interaction between a single bosonic mode and a spin which facilitates a state-dependent displacement. The lack of a Rabi interaction for propagating optical photons has rendered optical cat states elusive. Here, we show that the complex nonlinear scattering dynamics of a single-mode squeezed-vacuum state interacting with a quantum emitter can be engineered to produce a Rabi interaction between a quantum emitter and a propagating photon mode while the contributions from other orthogonal modes destructively interfere. Our protocol can deterministically prepare large-scale high-fidelity squeezed cat states from squeezed-vacuum pulses and is robust to photon loss due to spontaneous emission to non-guided modes. Extending to scattering multiple input squeezed-vacuum pulses off the quantum emitter, we propose generating linear cluster state strings with logical qubits encoded as squeezed cat states, which we refer as the cat cluster state. Our interaction scheme can potentially produce strings of entangled cat states at GHz rates using semiconductor quantum dots.

title: Cqlib: A High-Performance Software Stack for Quantum Computing
comment: 32 pages, 6 figures. A general-purpose and extensible software framework for quantum computing
summary: This paper presents Cqlib, a high-performance software stack for quantum computing built around a unified quantum circuit model. Its native Rust core provides efficient implementations of circuit processing, quantum-state and operator computation, compilation, and optimization, while Python and C interfaces support algorithm development and system integration. Cqlib covers quantum program construction, simulation, analysis, compilation, device adaptation, and result processing under consistent program semantics. Through OpenQASM and the Quantum Control Instruction Set (QCIS), Cqlib supports program representation and hardware-oriented execution. Cqlib further provides backend interfaces for device execution, with Cqlib-Tianyan serving as one implementation for QCIS-compatible quantum hardware. Evaluations using parameterized compilation tasks from Benchpress and related tests show that Cqlib achieves good functional coverage, compilation correctness, and execution efficiency within the evaluated task scope. We develop Cqlib-Algorithm as a modular library of reusable operators and composable components for widely used quantum algorithms, including quantum search, phase estimation, and variational algorithms, with additional support for error mitigation. To complement these building blocks with domain-specific workflows, we further develop Cqlib-VQE, Cqlib-QAOA, and Cqlib-QML for application-level studies in quantum chemistry, combinatorial optimization, and quantum machine learning, respectively. Cqlib also integrates source-grounded Skills and MCP-based tools to support agent-assisted program generation, backend execution, and result-guided workflow refinement. Overall, Cqlib provides a unified and extensible software foundation that connects quantum algorithm development, simulation, compilation, and execution on QCIS-compatible quantum hardware.

title: Multiphoton Electronic Coherences in Molecules
summary: We investigate multiphoton electronic coherences in a series of gas-phase atomic and molecular systems with increasing complexity. Our measurements are driven by pairs of phase-locked, deep-ultraviolet pulses with independent control of the relative phase and time delay. By combining the ionization yields measured at specific relative phases between the pulses, we can isolate different multiphoton orders and enable measurements of coherences between specific pairs of electronic states. We measure electronic coherences between states separated by zero-photon (i.e. within our laser bandwidth), one-photon and two-photons, resulting in signals with modulation periods ranging from 430 attoseconds to several femtoseconds. Fast electronic dynamics are tracked simultaneously with the accompanying nuclear motion. Additionally, we derive analytic expressions for the measured ionization yield as a function of pump-probe delay and demonstrate their use as a quantitative tool for isolating individual photon-order contributions within the total yield.

title: Spin-adapted state preparation for quantum chemistry
summary: Quantum phase estimation for strongly-correlated molecules requires an initial state of high overlap with the true ground state, and preparing one is a significant fault-tolerant cost. Matrix product states (MPS) produced by the density matrix renormalisation group (DMRG) are a leading choice, yet existing circuits treat their tensors as dense or do not use the full symmetries present in molecular electronic Hamiltonians. In quantum chemistry, DMRG also exploits total spin, a non-abelian symmetry, storing one amplitude per spin multiplet instead of one per state. We show that the reduced tensors of such a spin-adapted MPS, labelled by the steps of the unitary group approach, form an abelian-symmetric MPS, which existing block-sparse preparation protocols can load at a cost set by the multiplet count. One state-independent rotation per site, determined by a Clebsch-Gordan coefficient, then returns the state to the occupation basis. We provide resource estimates for our circuits on singlet ground states of active space models of iron-sulphur clusters, finding improvements in Toffoli count up to $135\times$ compared to dense methods and $4.9\times$ compared to block-sparse methods applied to the same states, with up to $3.7\times$ fewer ancilla qubits required.

title: Quantum Amplitude Estimation for Ligand and Pose Index Retrieval
comment: 45 pages, including 19 pages of Supplementary Information
summary: Structure-based virtual screening spans a combinatorial configuration space, motivating a quantum screening framework that targets threshold-qualified configuration indices without reconstructing a complete interaction-score table. Quantum amplitude estimation based on quantum phase estimation (QAE/QPE) supplies finite-resolution phase information to a reversible comparator that writes its decision to FLAG, while optional Grover-style quantum selection (QSEL) amplifies FLAG-selected outcomes and selector measurements identify the ligand, receptor state, rotation, and translation. In an ideal logical benchmark using AutoDock grid interactions as a proof-of-concept model, we evaluated initial FLAG acceptance probability, classification precision, shots required for 95% FLAG detection, and logical Q-operator calls across eight receptor systems and nested libraries of up to 1,024 ligand occupancies. Higher QAE/QPE resolution generally improved classification precision at additional evaluation cost, whereas suitably chosen QSEL iteration counts reduced required shots without improving classification precision, revealing selection and resource trade-offs for extending coherent index retrieval to more physically detailed molecular evaluation models.

title: Super-Multiplicativity of the Noncommutative Minimum and Applications to Quantum Privacy and Hypothesis Testing
summary: The hockey-stick divergence is a fundamental distinguishability measure in quantum information theory. It characterizes quantum differential privacy and determines the optimal error probability of binary quantum hypothesis testing with arbitrary priors. We study how it behaves on tensor-product states. To this end, we consider the noncommutative minimum $m(A,B):=(\mathrm{Tr}[A]+\mathrm{Tr}[B]-\|A-B\|_1)/2$ of positive semidefinite operators, which reduces to $\sum_x\min\{a_x,b_x\}$ when $A$ and $B$ commute, and we prove that it is super-multiplicative, i.e., $m(A\otimes C,B\otimes D)\ge m(A,B)\,m(C,D)$. As a consequence, we establish a sub-additivity property of the hockey-stick divergence on product states, in which the parameters of the individual systems are multiplied, and no additional prefactor appears. We show that this bound is tight, also for noncommuting states, and that it is strict for faithful states whenever at least two of the divergences are positive. Using this, we obtain sub-additivity of the Datta-Leditzky divergences, a parallel composition theorem for quantum differentially private channels under product neighboring inputs with at most linear degradation of the privacy parameters, and a sharp sub-additivity property of the hypothesis-testing relative entropy normalized by the acceptance probability. Finally, we apply the same tools to symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing. We determine the exact prefactor of the quantum Chernoff bound for every pair of noncommuting states satisfying mild conditions including a nonlattice condition and, under a quantitative version of this condition, the full asymptotic expansion to every fixed order in $1/n$, with explicitly computable coefficients. As a consequence, we determine the sample complexity of symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing up to one sample, as the error probability tends to zero.

title: Reconstructing Pure-State OTOCs from Forward-Time Linear Response
summary: We show that the connected out-of-time-ordered correlator (OTOC) of any pure state can be reconstructed exactly from commutator linear responses alone. The protocol requires no time reversal, no ancilla, no double copy, and no weak measurement: a unitary string pulse, forward many-body evolution, and a single local readout suffice. An average over a complete basis of pulse generators yields the OTOC exactly. We further show that the measurement can be made sparse by restricting the pulses to a fixed operator weight, which turns the truncation into an analytically controlled spectral filter: the deterministic bias can be computed before the experiment and cleanly separated from the statistical sampling variance. For Gaussian states, the finite-weight response is exactly proportional to the full OTOC after a known combinatorial rescaling. For quantum chaotic systems, the typical residual is suppressed as a power law in the sector size. Exact-diagonalization benchmarks in the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model and a nonintegrable Ising chain confirm these predictions.

title: Positive-partial-transpose structure of completely entangled subspaces and their complements
summary: A completely entangled subspace (CES) contains no product vectors, so every state supported on it is entangled. Whether such a subspace can support states with positive partial transpose (PPT) is a more subtle question. The normalized projector onto a CES may be NPT even if there exist PPT states supported on the CES. We investigate this distinction using a semidefinite criterion that optimizes the smallest partial-transpose eigenvalue over all supported density operators. For two- qutrit states supported on CESs, this leads to a complete characterization: a CES supports PPT states exactly when it is four-dimensional and related by invertible local transformations to the complement of an unextendible product basis (UPB). We also establish restrictions on PPT states whose ranges contain only vectors of Schmidt rank at least three, ruling out their existence in $3\otimes n$, $4\otimes4$, and $4\otimes5$, and showing that any such state in $4\otimes6$ must have rank eight. An interesting structure emerges when two orthogonal completely entangled subspaces together span the full Hilbert space, which we term \textit{complementary CESs}. Explicit constructions in $3\otimes4$ demonstrate that both subspaces can support PPT entanglement even when their normalized projectors are NPT. In $4\otimes4$, we construct a complementary pair whose normalized projectors are themselves PPT entangled. These constructions offer an alternative route to obtaining PPT entangled states, beyond the familiar approach based on UPB complements.

title: Remote Charging of Quantum Batteries via a Multimode Resonator
summary: We study the remote charging of a qubit battery by a qubit charger coupled through a finite multimode resonator. The charging protocol uses time-shifted coupling pulses that account for the spatial phases of the resonator modes. We compare the energy stored in the battery with its ergotropy, the maximum work extractable by a local unitary operation. In the single-excitation regime considered here, the battery stores energy at any nonzero excited-state population, but its ergotropy is positive only when that population exceeds one half. In the absence of loss, stronger coupling brings the battery above this threshold earlier, while the final charge remains nearly complete across the coupling range studied. For the parameters considered, qubit relaxation suppresses ergotropy more strongly than resonator loss at comparable decay rates. After the battery is disconnected, relaxation causes its stored energy to decay exponentially, yet its ergotropy vanishes at a finite time while half of its energy capacity remains occupied. For a fixed storage interval, disconnecting at the population maximum therefore preserves the most extractable work.

title: 500 Hz atom-atom entanglement distribution over metropolitan-scale fibers
summary: Quantum networks and repeaters are among the most promising routes to scale up quantum information systems. Nevertheless, various aspects still require significant improvement to achieve practical realization. Multiplexing can enhance the performance in many fundamental steps, thus emerging as a critical strategy for the realization of quantum repeaters. Currently, a major bottleneck in realizing functional quantum repeaters is heralded entanglement distribution over longdistance elementary links, as neither of the two dominant protocols-single-photon nor two-photon interference-can simultaneously achieve high efficiency and strong robustness. Here, we address this challenge by experimentally realizing a method that unifies the efficiency and robustness. By harnessing two 15 * 15 quantum memory arrays, we generate remote matter-matter entanglement at a rate of 546 Hz over 20 km of fiber without active phase stabilization. This rate exceeds that of two-photon and single-photon schemes by factors of 75,932 and 23, respectively, establishing a new benchmark for entangling speed over metropolitan-scale distances and enabling semi-deterministic entanglement distribution. Inherently compatible with multiplexed quantum repeater architectures, our scheme offers a promising approach towards the realization of future high-performance distributed quantum systems.

title: Observable-Level Expressivity in Fixed-Readout Quantum Neural Networks
summary: A central question in quantum machine learning is which functions of an input state a model can represent when its measurement is fixed by hardware or by experimental design. We address this question for quantum neural networks with a fixed readout observable, where the trainable pre-measurement dynamics determine the effective observable in the Heisenberg picture and the scalar output is the measured expectation value itself, without trainable affine post-processing. We characterize the reachable effective observables under three physical resource classes: unitary evolution, which preserves the spectrum of the readout; mixed-unitary evolution, which relaxes this to a majorization constraint while preserving the trace; and completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) evolution, whose Heisenberg adjoint is unital rather than trace-preserving and therefore lifts the trace constraint inherited at the mixed-unitary level. The three reachable sets are a fixed-spectrum orbit, its convex hull, and an operator interval, and the inclusions are strict for any readout that is not proportional to the identity. The separation is witnessed locally: for a fixed Pauli readout $Z_j$ on an arbitrary number of qubits, the amplitude-damping observable $γ\id+(1-γ)Z_j$ lies outside the mixed-unitary level for every $γ>0$. We realize the CPTP level with a Stinespring-channelized circuit and derive closed-form loss floors, $4γ^2/3$ and $γ^2$ for the unitary and mixed-unitary levels and zero at the CPTP level, which the numerics reproduce within precision. Structured-observable, Rényi-moment and classification experiments illustrate how the hierarchy manifests in finite-depth ansätze. The results identify which spectral constraint each physical resource relaxes, framing reachable-observable classes as a resource for expressivity rather than an architectural advantage.

title: Quantum simulation of low-temperature impurity models
summary: Quantum impurity models, which describe a small but strongly-interacting subsystem coupled to a large noninteracting bath, are the computational core of dynamical mean field theory and play an important role in simulating strongly correlated materials. We develop quantum algorithms for efficiently simulating these models at low temperatures and with high precision. For any impurity model on $n$ fermionic modes with fixed impurity size: (1) We give a quantum algorithm that prepares the thermal state at inverse temperature $β$ to precision $δ$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,β,\log(1/δ))$. This algorithm is the first to achieve both polynomial scaling in the inverse temperature and polylogarithmic scaling in the precision. When the Hamiltonian has an inverse-polynomial spectral gap, our quantum algorithm prepares its ground state to precision $δ$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log(1/δ))$. (2) We further give a quantum algorithm that prepares a purification of the thermal state in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,β,\log(1/δ))$. Using this purification, we estimate static and dynamical properties with error $δ$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $β$ and linear in $1/δ$ up to polylogarithmic factors, achieving the Heisenberg scaling. Our algorithms build on quantum Gibbs samplers, which are quantum analogues of Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. By using global jump operators instead of local ones, we avoid the $\exp(β)$ overhead commonly associated with quantum Gibbs samplers, making them efficient for impurity models even at low temperatures.

title: Combining Schrödinger and Heisenberg Evolution to Extend Quantum Many-Body Simulations
summary: Classical simulations of quantum many-body dynamics face complementary limitations: entanglement growth restricts state evolution in the Schrödinger picture, while operator spreading makes Heisenberg-picture calculations increasingly expensive. Here, we combine both approaches by evolving quantum states and observables independently and joining their dynamics through massively parallel tensor-network contractions. We implement this strategy using tree tensor networks and sparse Pauli propagation, extending evolution times beyond those reached by either method separately in our calculations. For a quench of the two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model at the critical field, we simulate the magnetization of an $11\times11$ open lattice up to $t=1.20$ by combining state and operator evolution over intervals $t_S=t_H=0.60$. We compare the dynamics with iPEPS, numerical linked-cluster expansion, and X-truncated sparse Pauli dynamics results. We also combine exact state evolution on small clusters with operator propagation on a larger lattice, improving agreement with iPEPS relative to cluster evolution alone. We further derive error bounds showing how the state can suppress operator errors and the evolved observable can reduce sensitivity to state errors.

title: Quantum Subentropy: Subadditivity and Sharp Bounds on Discrimination Error
summary:
Subentropy gives a tight spectral lower bound on the accessible information of ensembles of pure states. We prove its subadditivity for arbitrary bipartite states in finite dimensions and derive a sharp relation between conditional subentropy and the minimum discrimination error. This relation strengthens a conjectured comparison with conditional min-entropy. Its inverse gives the strongest universal lower bound on the error determined only by conditional subentropy and the number of labels. Both main results follow from a comparison of conditional subentropy with the average subentropy of measurement posteriors, valid for mixed signal states and every finite measurement. We characterize all equality cases in these two results and bound posterior deviations near equality. We also determine the optimal Lipschitz constant in trace distance for conditional subentropy on classical-quantum states, including the exact constant when the quantum marginal is fixed. A determinant inequality strengthens subadditivity and proves strong subadditivity for classical distributions, while an exact counterexample shows that strong subadditivity fails for quantum states.
  Lean 4 proofs of all theoretical results are available at https://pratikpatil.io/lean/subentropy/

title: Privacy-Enhanced Distributed Sensing Network via Causal-Order Switching and Probe Squeezing
comment: 27 pages in total. Main text: 15 pages, 5 figures. Supplementary material: 12 pages, 8 figures
summary: As sensor networks become more interconnected, sensitive information sharing among multiple users poses potential risks of information leakage, making privacy protection a critical challenge. To address this challenge, we quantify network privacy using the maximum information leakage ratio (MILR) and propose a protocol that enhances privacy through causal-order switching and probe squeezing. Causal-order switching harnesses intrinsic network propagation dynamics for privacy encoding, while probe squeezing suppresses information leakage through quantum channels and increases the information available for estimating the global parameter. These mechanisms enable an asymptotic exponential enhancement on the privacy with the squeezing rate. We experimentally demonstrate this mechanism in distributed beam-tilt sensing using spatially structured light without requiring nonclassical light sources. Our work identifies intrinsic network propagation dynamics as a resource for privacy protection and opens a new avenue for continuous-variable sensing networks that combine high precision with enhanced privacy.

title: Impact of structured noise on bosonic quantum error correction
summary: Bosonic quantum error correction relies on an accurate description of single-photon loss dissipation using an ideal annihilation operator, under which correctable loss errors act equivalently on different logical code states. In realistic weakly nonlinear bosonic modes, however, coupling to a structured environment can render photon loss Fock-state dependent, thereby modifying the effective dissipation operator and deforming the associated error space. Here, we experimentally investigate this effect in a three-dimensional circuit quantum electrodynamics system. By injecting spectrally engineered environmental noise into a weakly nonlinear oscillator, we observe pronounced frequency selectivity in the measured Fock-state dynamics. While the long-time transition rates converge to the Markovian limit, the transient dynamics display distinctly non-Markovian behavior, in quantitative agreement with a second-order time-convolutionless theory.
